concepts.title: Green functions: the response to a point source
concepts.explain: Imagine building a general source from many tiny point sources. First find the response to one unit point source, then add the responses by integration. This chapter follows the textbook convention $\Delta G=\delta$; with the alternative convention $-\Delta G=\delta$, every Green function changes its overall sign.
concepts.formula: \Delta G_d=\delta,\qquad G_1=\frac{|x-x_0|}{2},\quad G_2=\frac{\ln|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|}{2\pi},\quad G_3=-\frac1{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|}
concepts.conditions: The equality holds in the sense of distributions: the point source is included, while the function is harmonic away from it. An unbounded domain also needs a condition at infinity. In one dimension any affine function may be added; in two dimensions the logarithm needs a reference length.
concepts.proof:
First fix the sign convention $\Delta G=\delta$. Integrating over any small neighborhood of the source gives 1 on the right. The divergence theorem converts the left side to outward boundary flux. A fundamental solution must therefore be harmonic away from the source and have unit small-boundary flux. The following calculations cover three dimensions of space, with the point-source equality interpreted distributionally.

In three dimensions, let $R=|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|$. The radial equation away from the source is $(R^2G\prime)\prime=0$. Integrating gives $G=A+B/R$, so $G\prime=-B/R^2$. Multiplying by the sphere area $4\pi R^2$ gives flux $-4\pi B=1$, hence $B=-1/(4\pi)$. Choosing zero value at three-dimensional infinity sets $A=0$.

In two dimensions, the radial source-free equation is $(RG\prime)\prime=0$, giving $G=A+B\ln R$. The outward circular flux is $2\pi RG\prime=2\pi B$, hence $B=1/(2\pi)$. Write the logarithm as $\ln(R/R_*)/(2\pi)$ if a dimensionless argument is needed. The reference length $R_*$ changes only a constant; unlike the three-dimensional inverse distance, this logarithmic fundamental solution cannot decay at infinity.

In one dimension, $G\prime\prime=0$ on both sides of the source, so each side is a straight line. Continuity avoids an extra $\delta\prime$. Integration across the source gives $G\prime(x_0+)-G\prime(x_0-)=1$. The symmetric choice $G=|x-x_0|/2$ has right and left slopes $1/2,-1/2$, as required. Any $Ax+B$ may still be added. In all three cases, flux or a slope jump fixes the sign; one cannot attach the same remembered negative sign in every dimension.

example.question: Why is $1/(4\pi r)$ the wrong sign for this chapter's fundamental solution?
example.solution:
Test $g(r)=1/(4\pi r)$. It is harmonic for $r>0$, but this does not yet tell us whether its point source is positive or negative.

Its radial derivative is $g\prime=-1/(4\pi r^2)$. The flux through a sphere of radius $\epsilon$ is $4\pi\epsilon^2g\prime(\epsilon)=-1$. Therefore $\Delta g=-\delta$, which fails this chapter’s convention $\Delta G=+\delta$.

Changing the overall sign to $G=-1/(4\pi r)$ makes the flux $+1$. If the operator were instead $-\Delta$, the original positive reciprocal would be correct. Always write the operator convention first.

concepts.memory: One dimension: a V-shaped line. Two dimensions: a logarithm. Three dimensions: an inverse distance. Check the sign with flux.

sections.title: Dirichlet problems and the image method

concepts.title: Dirichlet Green functions and boundary integrals
concepts.explain: A Green function must produce one unit point source and satisfy a zero boundary condition. An image source is an imaginary helper placed outside the region being solved. Its job is to cancel the boundary value; it must not introduce another singularity inside the region.
concepts.formula: u(\mathbf r)=\int_VG(\mathbf r,\mathbf r\prime)f(\mathbf r\prime)\,dV\prime+\int_{\partial V}\varphi(\mathbf r\prime)\partial_{n\prime}G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r\prime)\,dS\prime
concepts.conditions: $\Delta_{r\prime}G=\delta(\mathbf r\prime-\mathbf r)$, $G|_{\partial V}=0$, $\Delta u=f$, and $u|_{\partial V}=\varphi$. Here n′ points out of the region. An exterior domain also needs suitable conditions at infinity.
concepts.proof:
Fix the observation point $\mathbf r$ and use $\mathbf r\prime$ as the integration variable. Choose $\Delta_{\mathbf r\prime}G=\delta(\mathbf r\prime-\mathbf r)$ and $G=0$ on the boundary. The first condition extracts the observation value; the second removes an unknown boundary derivative. Both are needed.

Start from Green’s second identity: $\int_V(u\Delta G-G\Delta u)dV\prime=\oint_{\partial V}(u\partial_{n\prime}G-G\partial_{n\prime}u)dS\prime$. Insert $\Delta u=f$ and the sampling property $\int u(\mathbf r\prime)\delta(\mathbf r\prime-\mathbf r)dV\prime=u(\mathbf r)$. The left side becomes $u(\mathbf r)-\int_VGf\,dV\prime$.

On the boundary, $G=0$ removes the otherwise unknown $\partial_{n\prime}u$ term, while the known value $u=\varphi$ leaves $\oint\varphi\partial_{n\prime}G\,dS\prime$. Move the source term to the right to get $u=\int_VGf\,dV\prime+\oint\varphi\partial_{n\prime}G\,dS\prime$. These are the source and boundary contributions.

This is the core derivation. To treat the singularity rigorously, remove a small ball around the observation point, integrate by parts, and shrink the ball; its boundary supplies the term $u(\mathbf r)$. The image method is only a way to construct a suitable $G$, and images must lie outside the domain. An unbounded domain also requires convergence and vanishing boundary terms at infinity. Normals always point outward from the region being solved.

example.question: How do we construct the Green function for a unit point source in the upper half-space with zero boundary values?
example.solution:
Place the real source at $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ with $y_0>0$, and its image at $(x_0,-y_0,z_0)$. For an observation point $(x,y,z)$, define $R^2=(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2+(z-z_0)^2$ and $R_*^2=(x-x_0)^2+(y+y_0)^2+(z-z_0)^2$.

Choose $G=-1/(4\pi R)+1/(4\pi R_*)$. At $y=0$, the squared distances are identical, so $G=0$. Only the first term has a source inside; the second term is harmonic throughout the upper half-space.

For prescribed plane values, differentiate with respect to the integration-source height using the downward outward normal. This gives the positive kernel $P=y/[2\pi((x-\xi)^2+y^2+(z-\zeta)^2)^{3/2}]$. With zero interior source, $u=\int_{\mathbb R^2}P\varphi\,d\xi d\zeta$. A constant $\varphi=C$ returns $u=C$, since the kernel integrates to 1.

concepts.memory: Check the operator, then the boundary, then infinity. The surface integral uses the outward normal.

sections.title: Green functions for different boundary conditions

concepts.title: Neumann compatibility, the arbitrary constant, and Robin boundaries
concepts.explain: Prescribing the normal derivative does not fix the overall constant in u. Before solving, check that the total source equals the total outward boundary flux. In a bounded domain, a Green function cannot satisfy both $\Delta G=\delta$ and zero normal derivative everywhere.
concepts.conditions: The domain is connected and bounded, with $\Delta u=f$ and $\partial_nu=g$. For the modified Neumann Green function, impose $\int_VG_N=0$ to fix its constant. Alternatively, keep $\Delta G=\delta$ and give G a compatible nonzero boundary flux. For a Robin condition, check whether the homogeneous problem has a nonzero solution.
concepts.proof:
First check the total balance. Integrate $\Delta u=f$ over the domain and apply the divergence theorem: $\int_Vf\,dV=\oint_{\partial V}\partial_nu\,dS=\oint_{\partial V}g\,dS$. The total source must equal total outward flux. If the totals differ, no function can satisfy the problem, so further solving is unnecessary.

Next explain the arbitrary constant. If $u_1,u_2$ have the same source and Neumann data, let $w=u_1-u_2$. Then $\Delta w=0,\partial_nw=0$. Integration by parts gives $\int_V|\nabla w|^2dV=\oint w\partial_nw\,dS-\int_Vw\Delta w\,dV=0$. Thus $\nabla w=0$, so $w$ is constant in a connected domain.

The Green function must satisfy the same balance. Requiring both $\Delta G=\delta$ and $\partial_nG=0$ would give $1=0$ after integration, so that bounded-domain construction is impossible. Instead use $\Delta G_N=\delta-1/|V|$. Its total source is $1-|V|/|V|=0$, compatible with zero normal derivative.

Impose $\int_VG_NdV=0$ to fix the Green function’s own constant. In Green’s formula, $\int u(\delta-1/|V|)dV=u-\bar u$, where $\bar u=|V|^{-1}\int_Vu\,dV$. The representation therefore determines the value relative to the mean. Prescribing the mean or one point value fixes the absolute value. This establishes the necessary balance and constant freedom; existence also relies on the relevant elliptic boundary-value theory.

Check homogeneous solutions separately for a Robin boundary. If the difference satisfies $\partial_nw+\alpha w=0$, its energy identity is $\int|\nabla w|^2=-\oint\alpha w^2$. If $\alpha\ge0$ and is strictly positive on part of the boundary, only $w=0$ is possible. Sign-changing or negative coefficients can admit resonances, so uniqueness is not automatic. Pure $\alpha=0$ returns to the Neumann constant freedom.

example.question: Does $u\prime\prime=1$ on $(0,L)$ with $u\prime(0)=u\prime(L)=0$ have a solution?
example.solution:
Integrate $u\prime\prime=1$ over $(0,L)$ to get $u\prime(L)-u\prime(0)=L$. Both prescribed derivatives are zero, making the left side zero. Since $L>0$, this is a contradiction and no solution exists.

If the conditions become $u\prime(0)=0,u\prime(L)=L$, the balance passes. Integrating once gives $u\prime=x+C_1$, and the left condition sets $C_1=0$. Integrating again gives $u=x^2/2+C_2$, which also satisfies the right condition.

The constant $C_2$ remains arbitrary because differentiation removes it. Requiring zero mean would give $L^{-1}\int_0^Lu\,dx=L^2/6+C_2=0$, fixing $C_2=-L^2/6$. This shows exactly what an extra normalization accomplishes.

concepts.memory: For flux-only boundaries, check the total balance first. Adding a constant does not change the flux.

sections.title: Green functions of the Helmholtz operator

concepts.title: Helmholtz fundamental solutions and radiation conditions
concepts.explain: For a time-harmonic wave, the radial fundamental solution is a spherical wave divided by distance. Both signs in the exponential satisfy the same point-source equation. The radiation condition selects one sign, and the time factor tells us which wave is outgoing.
concepts.conditions: $k>0$ in uniform, unbounded three-dimensional space. With the time factor $e^{-i\omega t}$, $e^{+ikR}/R$ is outgoing and satisfies $R(\partial_RG-ikG)\to0$. If the time factor is $e^{+i\omega t}$, the outgoing/incoming names are reversed.
concepts.proof:
Let $R$ be distance from the source. For $R>0$, the radial equation is $G\prime\prime+2G\prime/R+k^2G=0$. Set $v=RG$ and use $(RG)\prime\prime/R=G\prime\prime+2G\prime/R$ to reduce it to $v\prime\prime+k^2v=0$.

The constant-coefficient equation gives $v=Ae^{ikR}+Be^{-ikR}$, hence $G=(Ae^{ikR}+Be^{-ikR})/R$. Checking the equation only away from the source cannot determine $A,B$; these coefficients control wave direction and source strength.

As $R\to0$, expand to obtain $G=(A+B)/R+O(1)$. The small-sphere outward flux tends to $-4\pi(A+B)$, while $k^2\int_{R<\epsilon}GdV=O(\epsilon^2)\to0$. A unit source therefore requires $A+B=-1/(4\pi)$. Choosing $B=0$ or $A=0$ gives $G_\pm=-e^{\pm ikR}/(4\pi R)$. Together with the source-free equation, integration by parts around a removed ball establishes the distributional equality.

Selecting an outgoing wave requires a far-field condition. With time factor $e^{-i\omega t}$, the phase $kR-\omega t$ moves toward larger $R$, so the positive exponent is outgoing. Differentiation gives $\partial_RG_+-ikG_+=e^{ikR}/(4\pi R^2)$, hence $R(\partial_RG_+-ikG_+)\to0$. The negative exponent fails this outgoing condition.

The difference is $G_+-G_-=-i\sin(kR)/(2\pi R)$, whose origin limit is $-ik/(2\pi)$; it is a homogeneous solution without a point source. Different extra conditions thus select different fundamental solutions of the same equation. Replacing the time factor by $e^{+i\omega t}$ reverses the incoming and outgoing labels.

example.question: Why is checking the differential equation only for $R>0$ insufficient?
example.solution:
Test $g_C(R)=Ce^{ikR}/R$ with arbitrary $C$. For $R>0$, $v=Rg_C=Ce^{ikR}$ satisfies $v\prime\prime+k^2v=0$. Thus every value of $C$ passes the source-free check.

Near the source, however, $g_C=C/R+O(1)$, so its small-sphere flux is $-4\pi C$. Only $C=-1/(4\pi)$ gives a unit source. Taking $C=-1/(2\pi)$ produces source strength 2.

A fundamental-solution proof therefore needs two results: a zero equation away from the source, and unit flux normalization at the source. A radiation condition is a third check selecting outgoing or incoming behavior; it does not replace source normalization.

concepts.memory: Multiply the radial function by R to get a harmonic-oscillator equation. Use flux to fix the δ coefficient.

sections.title: Green functions of the wave equation

concepts.title: Retarded Green functions and causal response
concepts.explain: A wave travels at a finite speed. The response observed now comes from what the source did $R/c$ earlier. A retarded solution is causal: it cannot respond before the source acts or before the signal arrives.
concepts.formula: G_{\rm ret}=\frac{\delta(t-t\prime-R/c)}{4\pi c^2R},\qquad R=|\mathbf r-\mathbf r\prime|
concepts.conditions: Here the operator is $\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ in unbounded three-dimensional space, with zero initial response. For the operator $c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$, multiply the Green function by $c^2$. Nonzero initial displacement or velocity requires an additional homogeneous initial-value solution.
concepts.proof:
The core derivation uses Fourier transforms and distribution identities. Set $\tau=t-t\prime$ and use the spatial inverse convention $G=(2\pi)^{-3}\int e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R}\widehat G\,d^3k$. The operator $\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ becomes $\widehat G_{\tau\tau}+c^2|\mathbf k|^2\widehat G=\delta(\tau)$: each spatial frequency is an oscillator driven by a unit impulse.

Causality requires zero response for $\tau<0$. Integrating across zero makes the derivative jump by 1, while continuity avoids a $\delta\prime$. Thus $\widehat G=H(\tau)\sin(cq\tau)/(cq)$, with $q=|\mathbf k|$. Its value at $\tau=0+$ is 0 and its derivative is 1, satisfying both matching conditions.

In the inverse transform, choose the polar axis along $\mathbf R$. The angular integral is $4\pi\sin(qR)/(qR)$. Combining it with the measure $q^2dq$, for $R>0$ we obtain $G=H(\tau)/(2\pi^2cR)\int_0^\infty\sin(qR)\sin(cq\tau)dq$. The two denominator factors of $q$ cancel the $q^2$ in the measure.

Use the distribution identity $\int_0^\infty\sin(qR)\sin(cq\tau)dq=\pi[\delta(R-c\tau)-\delta(R+c\tau)]/2$. For $R>0,\tau\ge0$, the second term has no support. With $\delta(R-c\tau)=\delta(\tau-R/c)/c$, this gives $G_{\rm ret}=\delta(\tau-R/c)/(4\pi c^2R)$. The sine integral is not an ordinarily convergent integral; both the source point and wavefront are interpreted distributionally.

Superpose the Green function with the source. The time delta selects $t\prime=t-R/c$, so the zero-initial-response solution is $u(\mathbf r,t)=\int f(\mathbf r\prime,t-R/c)/(4\pi c^2R)dV\prime$, with the source start time respected. For the operator $c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$, multiply the response by $c^2$. Nonzero initial displacement or velocity requires an additional homogeneous initial-value solution.

example.question: A source $f(\mathbf r,t)=\delta(\mathbf r)H(t)$ starts acting continuously at the origin at t=0. What is the response with zero initial data?
example.solution:
Insert $f(\mathbf r\prime,t\prime)=\delta(\mathbf r\prime)H(t\prime)$ into the space-time convolution. The spatial delta fixes the source at the origin, a distance $R$ from the observation point, leaving $u(R,t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t-t\prime-R/c)H(t\prime)dt\prime/(4\pi c^2R)$.

The time delta selects $t\prime=t-R/c$. Its argument has derivative of absolute value 1 with respect to $t\prime$, so no extra factor of $c$ appears. Thus $u(R,t)=H(t-R/c)/(4\pi c^2R)$.

For $t<R/c$, the step is 0 and the signal has not arrived. For $t>R/c$, the step is 1 and the response is $1/(4\pi c^2R)$. Doubling the distance doubles the arrival time and halves the post-arrival strength. The source at $R=0$ and the wavefront itself require distributional or limiting interpretation.

concepts.memory: Choose the causal direction; replace the source time t by t−R/c; check the c² factor in the operator.

exercises.title: The Laplacian fundamental solution on the whole line
exercises.question: Find the Green function of the Laplacian on the unbounded one-dimensional line.
exercises.idea: Split the line at the source. Solve the homogeneous equation on each side, then join the two pieces using continuity and a derivative jump.
exercises.hint: Integrate $G\prime\prime=\delta(x-x_0)$ across the source to get $G\prime(x_0+)-G\prime(x_0-)=1$.
exercises.solution:
1. Away from the source, $G\prime\prime=0$, so G is affine on each side. A jump in G itself would produce δ′ in its second derivative. The equation contains only δ, so G must be continuous.

2. Choose a symmetric, translation-invariant fundamental solution $G=A|x-x_0|+B$. Its left and right derivatives are −A and A. Their jump is 2A, which must equal 1; therefore A=1/2. Choose the reference constant B=0.

3. In the distributional sense, $(|x-x_0|/2)\prime=\operatorname{sgn}(x-x_0)/2$. Differentiating once more gives δ, completing the check.

4. Any homogeneous solution may be added: $G=|x-x_0|/2+Ax+B$. No such one-dimensional fundamental solution tends to zero at both ends: zero slopes at both ends cannot produce a unit jump. Without extra conditions, the solution is not unique.
exercises.answer: $G(x,x_0)=|x-x_0|/2$ is the standard symmetric fundamental solution; an arbitrary $Ax+B$ may be added.
exercises.pattern: State the sign convention → solve in two pieces away from the source → require continuity to avoid δ′ → integrate to find the derivative jump → identify the homogeneous freedom.
exercises.pitfall: Do not copy the negative sign from three dimensions: $-|x-x_0|/2$ satisfies $-G\prime\prime=\delta$.
exercises.errata: The whole-line problem does not specify uniqueness conditions. The standard fundamental solution is a normalization choice; imposing decay at both ends would be impossible.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook problem; the corresponding instructor answer image was not available.

exercises.title: The Dirichlet solution of Poisson’s equation in the upper half-space
exercises.question: Solve $\Delta u=f(\mathbf r)$ in the three-dimensional half-space $y>0$, with $u(x,0,z)=\varphi(x,z)$.
exercises.idea: Reflect the source across the plane with the opposite sign. Then use Green’s identity to separate the volume-source term from the boundary Poisson kernel.
exercises.hint: The outward boundary normal is $-\mathbf e_y$; therefore $\partial_{n\prime}$ is not $+\partial_{y\prime}$.
exercises.solution:
Let the observation point be $\mathbf r=(x,y,z)$, the source point $\mathbf r\prime=(\xi,\eta,\zeta)$ with η>0, and the image point $(\xi,-\eta,\zeta)$. Write
$$R=\sqrt{(x-\xi)^2+(y-\eta)^2+(z-\zeta)^2},\quad R_* =\sqrt{(x-\xi)^2+(y+\eta)^2+(z-\zeta)^2}.$$

Choose $G=-1/(4\pi R)+1/(4\pi R_*)$. The real-source coefficient ensures $\Delta_{r\prime}G=\delta$. The image singularity is outside the domain. When η=0, R=R*, giving G=0. The function decays at infinity.

Green's second identity gives $u=\int_{\eta>0}Gf\,dV\prime+\int_{\eta=0}\varphi\partial_{n\prime}G\,dS\prime$. Differentiate the two terms on η=0 to obtain
$$\partial_{n\prime}G=-\partial_\eta G=\frac{y}{2\pi[(x-\xi)^2+y^2+(z-\zeta)^2]^{3/2}}.$$

Thus
$$u(x,y,z)=-\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\eta>0}\left(\frac1R-\frac1{R_*}\right)f(\xi,\eta,\zeta)\,d\xi d\eta d\zeta+\frac{y}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{\varphi(\xi,\zeta)}{[(x-\xi)^2+y^2+(z-\zeta)^2]^{3/2}}\,d\xi d\zeta.$$

Check the result: the volume term satisfies Poisson's equation and vanishes on the plane. The boundary kernel is positive, integrates to 1 over the plane, and concentrates at the observation point as y→0⁺. For continuous φ, the integral tends to φ. For example, f=0 and φ=C immediately give u=C. The formula requires convergence of the integrals and a chosen class of bounded/decaying solutions or specified far-field behavior that eliminates extra terms at infinity.
exercises.answer: The solution is the volume-source integral above plus the half-space Poisson integral, whose boundary kernel is $P=y/(2\pi[(x-\xi)^2+y^2+(z-\zeta)^2]^{3/2})$.
exercises.pattern: Draw the reflected point → subtract the image fundamental solution → check the boundary and interior source → calculate the outward normal derivative → apply Green’s formula → test a constant boundary value.
exercises.pitfall: The real-source fundamental solution has a negative inverse-distance sign, but the boundary kernel is positive. Without a far-field condition, harmonic functions such as cy can be added while keeping the zero plane boundary, destroying uniqueness.
exercises.errata: The problem specifies only the plane boundary. An unbounded domain also needs acceptable far-field behavior and convergent integrals; otherwise the solution is not unique.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook problem; the corresponding instructor answer image was not available.

exercises.title: The Poisson integral formula inside a disk
exercises.question: Solve $\Delta u=0$ inside a disk of radius a, with $u(a,\theta)=f(\theta)$.
exercises.idea: Use inversion in the circle to construct the two-dimensional Dirichlet Green function, then calculate its boundary normal derivative.
exercises.hint: The two-dimensional fundamental solution is logarithmic. Invert the source point to $\mathbf r_0^*=a^2\mathbf r_0/|\mathbf r_0|^2$.
exercises.solution:
1. Let the observation point be $\mathbf r_0=(\rho,\theta)$, 0<ρ<a, and let $\mathbf s$ be the integration point. Choose the two-dimensional Green function
$$G(\mathbf s,\mathbf r_0)=\frac1{2\pi}\ln\frac{a|\mathbf s-\mathbf r_0|}{\rho|\mathbf s-\mathbf r_0^*|},\qquad \mathbf r_0^*=\frac{a^2}{\rho^2}\mathbf r_0.$$
On |s|=a, $|\mathbf s-\mathbf r_0^*|=(a/\rho)|\mathbf s-\mathbf r_0|$, so G=0. The inverted point lies outside the disk; only the unit real source lies inside.

2. The outward normal points toward increasing |s|. Set |s|=s and $\psi=\theta\prime-\theta$. Differentiate both logarithmic distances radially and then set s=a:
$$\left.\partial_nG\right|_{s=a}=\frac{a^2-\rho^2}{2\pi a(a^2+\rho^2-2a\rho\cos\psi)}.$$

3. There is no volume source. The boundary arc element is $ds=a\,d\theta\prime$, so Green's formula gives
$$u(\rho,\theta)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{a^2-\rho^2}{a^2+\rho^2-2a\rho\cos(\theta-\theta\prime)}f(\theta\prime)\,d\theta\prime.$$

4. At ρ=0, take the limit to get the center mean value $u(0)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int f$, without using an image point at infinity. The Fourier expansion of the kernel is $1+2\sum_{n\ge1}(\rho/a)^n\cos n(\theta-\theta\prime)$. Every term is harmonic inside the disk and the kernel integrates to 2π. The radial boundary limit restores continuous f; at a jump, it gives the mean of the two one-sided limits.

5. Test $f=\cos m\theta$. Orthogonality immediately gives $u=(\rho/a)^m\cos m\theta$, agreeing with separation of variables.
exercises.answer: $u(\rho,\theta)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{a^2-\rho^2}{a^2+\rho^2-2a\rho\cos(\theta-\theta\prime)}f(\theta\prime)\,d\theta\prime$. The center value is the boundary mean.
exercises.pattern: Invert to locate the image → adjust the logarithmic constant to make the boundary zero → calculate the outward derivative → multiply by the arc element → test a constant or a single Fourier mode.
exercises.pitfall: The boundary derivative contains 1/a and the arc element contains a. They cancel in the final formula; dropping either factor gives incorrect dimensions.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook problem; the corresponding instructor answer image was not available.

exercises.title: The Dirichlet Green function outside a sphere
exercises.question: Use the image method to find the Green function for the first boundary-value problem of Poisson’s equation outside a sphere of radius a. Compare it with Example 5.2.2.
exercises.idea: Invert the exterior real source into the sphere. The ratio of the two distances on the sphere determines the image strength.
exercises.hint: If the real source is at distance b>a from the center, its image lies at distance a²/b and has strength ratio −a/b.
exercises.solution:
Put the sphere center at the origin. Let the real source $\mathbf r_0$ satisfy b=|r₀|>a. Its inverted image $\mathbf r_0^*=a^2\mathbf r_0/b^2$ lies inside the sphere. Set
$$G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r_0)=-\frac1{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|}+\frac{a}{4\pi b|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0^*|}.$$

On the sphere |r|=a, $|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0^*|=(a/b)|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|$, so the terms cancel. The negative inverse-distance real-source term gives $\Delta_rG=\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0)$. The image lies outside the region being solved and introduces no interior point source. As r→∞, G→0, satisfying exterior decay. The exterior Dirichlet uniqueness theorem therefore identifies this as the required Green function.

Compare with Example 5.2.2. For a real exterior electric charge q in permittivity ε₀, the physical Poisson equation must be $\Delta\Phi=-(q/\varepsilon_0)\delta$. Hence
$$\Phi=-\frac q{\varepsilon_0}G=\frac q{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac1{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|}-\frac{a/b}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0^*|}\right].$$
The image charge is $q_*=-qa/b$ at $\mathbf r_0^*$. This is the image potential for the grounded conducting sphere in Example 5.2.2. That example uses a Legendre expansion mode by mode; the image method satisfies the boundary in one construction. Uniqueness explains why both methods agree.

Check the leading far field: $\Phi\sim[q(1-a/b)]/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r)$, corresponding to the algebraic sum of the real and image charges. If a uniform field or constant potential is prescribed at infinity, add the appropriate harmonic solution separately.
exercises.answer: $G=-1/(4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|)+a/(4\pi b|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0^*|)$, $\mathbf r_0^*=a^2\mathbf r_0/b^2$. The physical image charge is $-qa/b$.
exercises.pattern: Invert to find the location → use the sphere-distance ratio for the coefficient → check real-source normalization → check the boundary and infinity → compare potentials using Φ=−qG/ε₀.
exercises.pitfall: For an exterior sphere, the image must be inside the sphere. The image term in G is positive, but the physical image charge is negative because Φ=−qG/ε₀.
exercises.errata: The point-source sign in Example 5.2.2, Eq. (5.2.97), is inconsistent with its positive-charge Coulomb potential. Use the physical convention $\Delta\Phi=-\rho_e/\varepsilon_0$ when comparing, while retaining this chapter's convention $\Delta G=\delta$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook problem; the corresponding instructor answer image was not available.

exercises.title: Verifying both Helmholtz point-source fundamental solutions
exercises.question: Prove that both functions $G_\pm(r)=-e^{\pm i\omega r}/(4\pi r)$ given in textbook Eq. (6.4.15) solve Eq. (6.4.8), namely $(\Delta+\omega^2)G_\pm=\delta(\mathbf r)$.
exercises.idea: Check two separate things: the homogeneous equation away from the source, and the δ normalization at the source.
exercises.hint: For a radial function, $\Delta g=(rg)\prime\prime/r$ when r>0. The small-sphere flux determines the δ coefficient.
exercises.solution:
1. For r>0, set $v_\pm=rG_\pm=-e^{\pm i\omega r}/(4\pi)$. Direct differentiation gives $v_\pm\prime\prime=-\omega^2v_\pm$, so $\Delta G_\pm+\omega^2G_\pm=0$.

2. Near r=0, expand: $G_\pm=-1/(4\pi r)\mp i\omega/(4\pi)+O(r)$. Both have the same singular leading term. Thus $\partial_rG_\pm=1/(4\pi r^2)+O(1)$, and on a sphere of radius ε,
$$\oint_{r=\varepsilon}\partial_rG_\pm\,dS=1+O(\varepsilon^2)\to1.$$
Also $\omega^2\int_{r<\varepsilon}G_\pm\,dV=O(\varepsilon^2)\to0$.

3. The operator therefore produces a unit point source at the origin and zero elsewhere. More rigorously, take a smooth compactly supported test function ψ and integrate by parts in the region with a small sphere removed. The inner-boundary limit leaves only ψ(0), giving $\langle(\Delta+\omega^2)G_\pm,\psi\rangle=\psi(0)$. Both functions satisfy the required distributional equation.

4. Their difference $G_+-G_-=-i\sin(\omega r)/(2\pi r)$ has a finite limit at the origin and satisfies the homogeneous equation. The equation alone cannot select the sign; a radiation condition is needed. With the time factor $e^{-i\omega t}$, + is outgoing. If the textbook uses $e^{+i\omega t}$, the outgoing/incoming names are reversed.
exercises.answer: Both functions satisfy $(\Delta+\omega^2)G=\delta$: each solves the homogeneous equation away from the source and has small-sphere flux tending to 1.
exercises.pattern: Multiply the radial function by r → differentiate twice to check the homogeneous equation → expand the singular part → fix the δ coefficient by flux → state the radiation condition.
exercises.pitfall: A calculation only for r>0 cannot prove an inhomogeneous point-source equation. Outgoing/incoming names depend on the time convention, not just on the spatial exponential.
